items.title: Trump Takes a Bulldozer to Birthright Citizenship Again
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. If at first you don’t succeed, appeal to a higher federal court. And if you even lose at the Supreme Court … just try again anyway. This seems to be President Trump’s approach to limiting birthright citizenship. Last year, he issued an executive order that purports to end the practice of automatically granting citizenship to babies born in the United States—as has been the norm since the late 19th century. Despite Trump visiting oral arguments in an apparent attempt to intimidate the justices, the Supreme Court struck down the order this June. Yesterday, Trump attempted to do some of the same things via new executive orders. One is intended to deny automatic citizenship to children born to people living in the United States while working for a foreign government and children of people declared to be terrorists or adversaries of the U.S. It would also deny citizenship to people born in U.S. territories if Congress passes a proposed law allowing that, creating a new group of stateless people. The second order is intended to prevent the practice of “birth tourism,” in which people visiting the United States on tourist visas give birth to babies who are then U.S. citizens. Legal experts and advocates say the orders are unconstitutional, and they are certain to be challenged in court. Trump’s loss at the Supreme Court seems to make these orders a long shot. As Chief Justice John Roberts wrote in his opinion for the Court , “children born of parents unlawfully or temporarily present in the United States” satisfy the relevant conditions and thus “under the Constitution, they are citizens at birth.” The language in the orders about “alien enemies” is another likely area for dispute, not because anyone is eager to welcome the children of bona fide adversaries but because this administration has made absurd claims about illegal immigration constituting an “invasion,” which makes no sense on its face and has been rejected by federal judges. Trump’s announcement of the orders at the White House yesterday was full of fabrications, exaggerations, and lies. Trump claimed that the Fourteenth Amendment “was meant for the babies of slaves. It was—it was right after—one week or two weeks after the Civil War ended.” In fact, it passed three years later, in 1868. The presidential adviser Stephen Miller echoed the same idea, saying that the amendment “had no other meaning and purpose outside of that, and that’s been clear, obviously, since the day that it was passed.” When a politician uses the word obviously —like frankly —that’s a good sign that what follows will be neither obvious nor true. If this had been obvious since 1868, the U.S. wouldn’t have acted otherwise for more than a century, and the Supreme Court would have ruled in favor of the administration. Trump’s claims about birth tourism were even further off base. The president isn’t making the idea up—just wildly exaggerating it. Asked by a reporter how many people are engaging in the practice, Trump said, “I can tell you right now. Hundreds of thousands. Hundreds of thousands.” This number appears to be pulled out of thin air. During Supreme Court oral arguments, Solicitor General John Sauer, arguing on behalf of Trump, was asked how commonly birth tourism occurs and replied, “No one knows for sure.” In 2020, the Center for Immigration Studies, which supports much stricter laws, estimated the number at between 20,000 and 26,000 births each year, out of roughly 3.6 million babies born in the United States. By attempting to end or restrict birthright citizenship in order to address these issues, Trump is trying to use a bulldozer to achieve a task that calls for a small mallet. The law already prohibits fraudulent visa applications, and the Justice Department has prosecuted people for birth tourism in the past. Trying to undermine birthright citizenship risks jettisoning one of the fundamental bases of modern American society to deal with a minor challenge. Trump could have tried another path. Justice Brett Kavanaugh offered the White House a potential lifeline in his concurrence in the birthright case, suggesting that despite the plain language of the Fourteenth Amendment, Congress could pass a law altering birthright citizenship. The likelihood of such a bill succeeding seems very low, and pushing it through would require sustained attention from Trump. Instead, he’s trying to achieve his goals through executive orders, which are both easily reversed by a future president and have already proved unsuccessful. But the president has a demonstrated weakness for this kind of grand, overreaching presidential gesture. Last month, after a member of the U.S. men’s national soccer team was suspended for a game in the World Cup, Trump decided to use his position to exert some pressure , calling FIFA President Gianni Infantino to try to get the suspension waived. In a direct sense, it worked—FIFA allowed the player to participate—but it may have backfired. Belgium, the American opponent, was incensed, and trounced the United States 4–1. Trump ended up looking obnoxious and corrupt, but didn’t even get a victory out of it. The player in question, by the way, was Folarin Balogun—a U.S. citizen by birth because his mother, while pregnant and visiting family, got stuck in the United States. Related: The revolutionary idea that remade the New World The other case for birthright citizenship Here are four new stories from The Atlantic : MAGA’s most famous prisoner is free. Icarus in the faculty lounge Bring back the blue-book exam. Sadism and a blue bunny Today’s News Senator Bill Cassidy said he will vote for Todd Blanche to be the next attorney general, giving Republicans enough support to confirm President Trump’s nominee despite opposition from GOP Senators Lisa Murkowski and Susan Collins. The U.S. economy unexpectedly lost 23,000 jobs in July , while the Labor Department lowered May and June’s job figures by a combined 103,000, adding to signs that the labor market is weakening. A 14-year-old student in Thailand killed his grandparents and fatally shot five teachers and staff members at a school outside Bangkok , before dying by suicide, authorities said. Twenty-three people were wounded, nine critically, and Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said the government would pursue a stricter gun law following the country’s second school shooting this year. Explore all of our newsletters here. Evening Read Illustration by Dena Springer A Chatbot-Free Childhood Will Be a Status Symbol By Dana Suskind The human brain has evolved to learn from specific instructors. When a child hears a gentle spoken word or a soothing lullaby from another person, when their cry is responded to, their brain lights up. Nurturing interactions, or what child-development experts call “serve and return” exchanges, help shape and strengthen the 1 million new neural connections taking place in a child’s brain every single second. Every time a child cries or serves up a bid for attention and receives a caregiver’s response, that back-and-forth helps build the circuits underlying their communication, learning, and emotional well-being. No other input, not even Johann Pachelbel’s Canon in D performed by the Berlin Philharmonic, is capable of activating the neural circuitry the way human interaction does. Until now. items.title: Fada N’Gourma : Le CICR mise sur les médias pour renforcer l’accès à une information humanitaire de qualité
items.description: Le Comité international de la Croix-Rouge (CICR) a réuni, le mercredi 5 août 2026 à Fada N’Gourma, des journalistes des régions du Grand Est et du Nakambé pour un atelier d’échanges consacré à l’action humanitaire. Cette rencontre, couplée à une visite de terrain, visait à permettre aux professionnels des médias de mieux comprendre les interventions du Mouvement international de la Croix-Rouge et du Croissant-Rouge au Burkina Faso, afin de diffuser une information plus juste et plus utile aux populations. Au cours de cette immersion, les journalistes ont découvert plusieurs réalisations du CICR dans la région de l’Est. Première étape, le Centre hospitalier régional universitaire (CHRU) de Fada N’Gourma, où l’organisation intervient depuis 2022 pour renforcer la prise en charge des blessés. L’appui porte notamment sur la fourniture de consommables médicaux, le renforcement des capacités du personnel soignant ainsi que la construction d’un Centre de récupération et d’éducation nutritionnelle (CREN). Pour Jean-Louis Bamboulé, Professeur chirurgien et représentant du directeur général du CHRU, ce partenariat a considérablement renforcé les capacités de l’établissement. « Le CICR est un partenaire déterminé venu en appui au CHRU de Fada », Jean-Louis Bamboulé « Le CICR est un partenaire déterminé venu en appui au CHRU de Fada, qui accueille un nombre important de patients. En plus des médicaments, il y a des infrastructures et des sessions de renforcement des capacités au profit des agents », a-t-il souligné. La délégation s’est ensuite rendue au Centre de santé et de promotion sociale (CSPS) du secteur 11, désormais érigé en Centre médical urbain grâce à l’accompagnement du CICR. Dans cette zone qui accueille un grand nombre de personnes déplacées internes, l’organisation a également réalisé un forage d’un débit de 2,10 m³ par heure afin d'améliorer l’accès à l’eau potable. Cette infrastructure, inscrite dans les actions Eau, Hygiène et Assainissement (WASH), contribue à répondre aux besoins essentiels des communautés vulnérables. Les bénéficiaires rencontrés sur place ont exprimé leur satisfaction et leur gratitude envers le CICR, saluant des interventions qui améliorent concrètement leurs conditions de vie. Pour Zalissa Sanfo, chargée de communication publique au CICR, cette initiative répond à une volonté de rapprocher les journalistes des réalités du terrain afin qu’ils puissent mieux relayer les enjeux humanitaires. « Avec les journalistes, nous avons fait le plaidoyer pour que la bonne information puisse accéder aux personnes », Zalissa Sanfo « Avec les journalistes, nous avons fait le plaidoyer pour que la bonne information puisse accéder aux personnes. La bonne information, au bon moment, à la bonne personne, peut être perçue comme une aide humanitaire et peut sauver une vie » , a-t-elle déclaré. Au-delà de la visite des réalisations, les participants ont bénéficié d'une présentation sur les principes, les missions et le fonctionnement du Mouvement international de la Croix-Rouge et du Croissant-Rouge. Ils ont également été informés de l’organisation prochaine du concours de reportage humanitaire du CICR, une initiative destinée à encourager les productions médiatiques mettant en lumière les questions humanitaires et les défis auxquels font face les populations affectées. À travers cette rencontre, le CICR réaffirme sa conviction que les médias constituent des partenaires essentiels dans la diffusion d'une information fiable, responsable et susceptible de contribuer à la protection des populations en situation de vulnérabilité. items.title: Luv FM High School Debate: Twenty schools get set to battle for 2026 crown
items.description: Twenty Senior High Schools in the Ashanti Region are set to compete for the ultimate prize in the eighth edition of the LUV FM High School Debate, powered by Kelcharcoal. The annual intellectual competition begins on Monday, August 10, 2026, after more than 100 schools participated in preliminary contests held across the region. The schools were grouped into zones during the preliminary phase, with the top 20 emerging as finalists after a series of competitive debates. The finalists will compete by demonstrating their skills in public speaking, critical thinking and teamwork, with judges assessing participants based on the structure and clarity of arguments, presentation skills, technical accuracy and overall delivery. Relationship Manager at LUV FM, Maxwell Frimpong-Manso, said the competition has grown into an important platform for developing young people beyond the classroom. “Over the years, the LUV FM Kelcharcoal debate has grown in stature and impact. While only one school will be crowned, every participant will leave with valuable knowledge and confidence. Multimedia remains committed to providing quality content and empowering our communities.” Chairperson and Ambassador of the LUV FM High School Debate, Theodosia Jackson, said the increasing participation from schools reflects the relevance and popularity of the programme. She encouraged more schools to join future editions, describing the debate as a platform that helps students build confidence and prepare for future challenges. “The competition, I have realised, has attracted many participants. It shows the programme’s popularity and interest. We are asking schools to register and take advantage of gaining knowledge, confidence and boldness to face challenges in life. It is a training ground for our students.” Lead Judge and Senior Lecturer at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) Department of English, Dr Peter Arthur, said the judging process this year would focus more on the technical strength of arguments. He explained that participants would be assessed beyond emotional appeal, with emphasis placed on logic, organisation and evidence-based presentations. “This year, we will look out for technicalities and focus also on the structure of arguments rather than emotions. The expectation is very high. They are smart, and so it leaves us with a lot to expect.” Regional SRC President, Hope Arthur James, said the partnership between the Ashanti Regional Students’ Council and LUV FM has helped create opportunities for students to develop their communication skills. “Our commitment as ARSRC was to advocate for students and liaise between institutions and the student body. LUV FM-Kelcharcoal provided a very viable space for us to materialise that commitment. The past eight years have been able to bring out the best in Ashanti Regional students.” The 2026 edition is sponsored by Kelcharcoal toothpaste, Didi Shito, Bigoo, The Seed Travelz, Serpo Mystical Pen, Verna Mineral Water, Jackson University College, Tamak, St. Ben Jewelry, Otuasekan Community Bank and New Generation Investment Services. Organisers say the debate remains committed to nurturing young talents and providing students with a platform to sharpen skills that are essential for leadership and national development.

items.title: Gender Minister begins Northern Region tour to monitor LEAP enrolment exercise
items.description: The Minister for Gender, Children and Social Protection, Dr Agnes Naa Momo Lartey, has begun a three-day working visit to the Northern and North East regions to monitor the ongoing Livelihood Empowerment Against Poverty (LEAP) beneficiary enrolment exercise and engage key stakeholders on the implementation of the programme. The Minister is accompanied by members of the Ministry’s Advisory Board and senior management staff as part of the exercise, which is aimed at assessing the progress of the nationwide LEAP enrolment and expansion programme. As part of the first day’s activities, Dr Lartey paid a courtesy call on the Chief of Fuo, Abdulai Neindow, in the Sagnarigu Municipality before visiting the community’s LEAP enrolment centre. At the enrolment centre, she interacted with beneficiaries, registration officials and community members while observing the registration process to assess the efficiency of operations and ensure that eligible households are enrolled in a transparent and orderly manner. Addressing the media, the Minister said the monitoring exercise forms part of the Ministry’s commitment to ensuring the successful implementation of the expanded LEAP programme, which seeks to enrol an additional 400,000 beneficiary households across the country. She explained that the exercise provides an opportunity to assess field operations, identify operational challenges and implement timely interventions to improve service delivery. Dr Lartey also highlighted the importance of the nationwide LEAP reassessment, noting that it is intended to update beneficiary data, strengthen the integrity of the programme and ensure that support reaches the most vulnerable households. According to her, the reassessment will help minimise inclusion and exclusion errors while promoting fairness, accountability and effective targeting of social protection interventions. The Minister’s three-day tour will also include engagements with stakeholders across the Northern and North East regions, as well as a visit to the Gambaga Alleged Witches Camp.

items.title: Crise migratoire à Sebta : l’AMDH réclame une enquête pour déterminer les responsabilités
items.description: L'Association marocaine des droits humains (AMDH) a appelé, vendredi, à l’ouverture d’une enquête indépendante et globale concernant les événements de Sebta et Melilla occupées survenus les 30 et 31 juillet. Selon l'association, le bilan des morts s'élèverait à 141 cas et 11 nationalités arabes faisaient partie des migrants. Lors d'une conférence de presse organisée au siège de l’AMDH à Rabat, en partenariat avec la Coordination européenne pour les droits humains au Maroc, l'organisation a appelé à déterminer les différentes responsabilités, élucider les circonstances des événements précités et décider des suites juridiques. La présidente de l’AMDH, Souad Brahma, a en ce sens estimé que sur la base des témoignages recueillis auprès des personnes revenues et du suivi effectué par les acteurs de terrain, « le nombre annoncé de victimes ne reflète pas la réalité ». Selon les chiffres avancés par l'association, le bilan des décès suivant les tentatives de rejoindre Sebta occupée serait de 141 morts. Pour l'AMDH, ces événements « ne constituent pas seulement une tentative de franchissement de frontière, mais révèlent la profondeur de la crise sociale au Maroc », avec une dimension politique marquée par « l’effondrement des institutions de médiation et l’affaiblissement du rôle d’encadrement des partis politiques et des syndicats » . Souad Brahma a affirmé que « les événements tragiques de Sebta et Melilla occupées nécessitent l’ouverture d’une enquête indépendante et transparente », considérant qu’ils traduisent « une crise et un échec des politiques publiques, au point que la mer est devenue plus clémente que l’État ». Qualifiant les faits de « grande tragédie humaine », l'organisation de défense des droits humains a critiqué l’absence de proclamation d’un deuil national. Par ailleurs, la présidente a pointé du doigt l’explication avancée par le porte-parole du ministère de l’Intérieur, qui avait évoqué l’implication de réseaux de traite des êtres humains. Elle a considéré que cela s'apparentait à un recours à « la théorie du complot », tout en critiquant que les personnes revenues soient confrontées à l’emprisonnement plutôt qu’à une prise en charge. En ce sens, l'AMDH et la Coordination européenne pour les droits humains au Maroc ont également fait état de la situation judiciaire de plusieurs candidats à la migration. Selon elles, 59 personnes sont placées en détention provisoire à Tétouan, dont 5 mineurs, tandis que 52 autres sont détenues à Nador, parmi lesquelles 18 mineurs placés dans un centre de protection de l’enfance. Elles évoquent également 11 personnes poursuivies devant la Cour d’appel de Nador pour des chefs d’accusation criminels, notamment entrave à la circulation, violences contre des agents publics et rébellion collective. De son côté, Achraf Maimoun, président de la section de l’AMDH à Tétouan, a affirmé que « la tragédie avait commencé avant le 30 juillet », en soulignant qu’une tentative de franchissement impliquant plus de 500 personnes avait été enregistrée le 27 juillet, selon des données documentées par la partie espagnole de Sebta occupée. A ce titre, il a signalé que des familles contactaient l’association depuis mai dernier pour signaler qu’elles n’avaient toujours pas récupéré les corps de leurs proches. Le représentant associatif a également estimé que la partie marocaine « n’avait pas lancé une opération de recherche massive des corps » , en se limitant selon lui à récupérer les dépouilles flottant à la surface de l’eau. Il a déclaré qu'actuellement 21 corps se trouvaient dans une morgue, dont ceux de migrants issus de 11 nationalités arabes. « Ce ne sont pas des chiffres, ce sont des personnes qui avaient des rêves et qui voulaient vivre dignement », a-t-il déclaré, estimant qu’elles avaient péri « devant les autorités des deux pays, sans intervention qui aurait pu réduire le nombre de victimes » . Dans les documents distribués lors de la conférence de presse, l’AMDH a également avancé le rôle et l'impact des politiques européennes en matière de migration dans ces événements. L'AMDH a ainsi critiqué « les politiques européennes jugées inhumaines dans la gestion des questions migratoires » , estimant qu’elles auraient transformé les migrants en « instrument politique utilisé par certaines forces de droite européennes pour renforcer leur influence et masquer les véritables causes des crises sociales touchant une partie des populations européennes » . Enfin, l'association a estimé que « la tragédie de Sebta et Melilla ne peut être dissociée de la nature inégale et injuste des relations entre les pays du Nord et du Sud, et des déséquilibres économiques et sociaux qui en résultent » . items.title: 2027: Kefas picks APC women leader as running mate
items.description: By Femi Bolaji JALINGO — Taraba State Governor, Dr Agbu Kefas, has indicated that the Deputy National Women Leader of the All Progressives Congress (APC), Zainab Ibrahim, may be his running mate in the 2027 governorship election. Kefas made the disclosure on Friday at the TY Danjuma House in Jalingo while hosting the National Chairman of the APC, Prof Nentawe Yilwatda. Yilwatda was in the state to celebrate his 58th birthday. While recognising dignitaries during the protocol session, Governor Kefas referred to Ibrahim as the “future deputy governor of Taraba State”, a description also used by the APC national chairman, who addressed her as the “incoming deputy governor”. In his remarks, Kefas expressed appreciation to the APC leadership for organising a state-wide medical outreach as part of activities marking Yilwatda’s birthday. According to him, “Your team of doctors for the free treatment and surgeries has been on the ground working for days, and the testimonies from the people of Taraba State are deeply impressive. “For us in Taraba State, we are all for the APC to pay back what Mr President has done for us. “What President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has done for the people of Taraba cannot be quantified. “Mr President recently approved an Army division for us, which alone is capable of stabilising the state. Mr Chairman, here in Taraba, we in the APC are not contesting elections with anybody. We only have people participating with us.” Speaking earlier, Yilwatda explained that he chose Taraba State for his 58th birthday celebration to demonstrate the party’s commitment to the welfare of citizens. According to him, “APC does not only canvass for votes but also show the human face of our party. “We do not only knock on doors for votes, but we care for the people’s health, education and future.” He also commended Governor Kefas for aligning with the ruling party, noting that President Tinubu prioritises inclusive development irrespective of past electoral outcomes. items.title: Nouveau BMS canicule en Algérie : jusqu’à 45°C, les régions concernées
items.description: Les alertes à la canicule se succèdent en Algérie. Depuis un mois, la vague de chaleur frappe de plein fouet plusieurs régions du pays. Le dernier BMS (bulletin météorologique spécial) de canicule en date a été lancé ce vendredi 7 août par l’Office national de la météo (ONM). Placée sous vigilance orange canicule (niveau II), Bejaïa, Skikda, Annaba, El Tarf et Jijel. Ces cinq wilayas du littoral seront confrontées à des températures élevées de 40°C à 42°C dans la journée, et de 26°C à 28°C dans la soirée, et ce du dimanche au lundi 10 août. Algérie : canicule et incendies, un été pourri La deuxième alerte lancée par l’ONM concerne les wilayas de Chlef, Relizane et Aïn Defla, où les températures peuvent atteindre 45°C dans la journée. En soirée, il fera très chaud et le mercure pourrait grimper jusqu’à 30°C, et ce durant trois jours : samedi, dimanche 09 et lundi 10 août. Cette nouvelle vague de chaleur qui touche huit wilayas du pays survient alors que les incendies continuent de ravager les forêts du pays. Ce vendredi, dans son dernier point de situation, la Protection civile a indiqué avoir enregistré 15 incendies, dont 12 ont été éteints et trois sont toujours en activité à Tipaza, Jijel et Souk Ahras. items.title: Patchbay Band to share their story on E Vibes this August
items.description: Patchbay Band, one of Ghana’s most celebrated live music ensembles, will feature on E Vibes this August, sharing the story behind their remarkable journey and contributions to Ghana’s music industry. Like a patchbay in a recording studio that connects different instruments, hardware and signals into one unified sound, Patchbay Band has become a musical connector in its own right. Formed in 2008 by bassist and music director Philip Acquah, the Accra-based band is renowned for blending traditional Ghanaian highlife with jazz, blues and indie rock. The award-winning group has headlined performances at the iconic +233 Jazz Bar, served as the backing band for the Ghana Music Awards, and shared the stage with artistes including Sarkodie, Stonebwoy and Wiyaala. They have also released original songs such as “3y3 Life” and “Sanbra.” They will tell their story on JoyNews on Saturday, 15th August at 4:00 pm, with a repeat on Sunday at 10:30 am and Friday at 6:30 pm. The programme will also air on JoyPrime on Saturday, 15th August at 4:30 pm. E Vibes, the JoyNews programme that delves into the backgrounds of celebrated personalities excelling in their chosen fields, is focusing this season on music bands in Ghana. Dubbed #MusicalBandSeries, the programme celebrates the journeys, triumphs, challenges and enduring bonds of Ghanaian musical bands. The show takes viewers through the defining moments of each band’s rise, with the hope that their inspiring stories will preserve Ghana’s musical heritage and motivate the next generation.

items.title: Amine Harit repousse une offre qatarie et privilégie l'OM
items.description: L'avenir d'Amine Harit reste incertain à l'Olympique de Marseille (OM), mais le milieu offensif marocain n'envisage pas, à ce stade, un départ. Alors qu'un club qatari s'est récemment manifesté pour s'attacher ses services, le Lion de l'Atlas privilégierait la poursuite de son aventure sur la Canebière. Selon plusieurs médias, Harit espère profiter du remaniement de l'effectif marseillais cet été pour retrouver du temps de jeu. Convaincu de pouvoir encore apporter à l'équipe, il compte sur les départs annoncés au sein du groupe pour rebattre les cartes et convaincre le staff technique de lui accorder une nouvelle chance après une saison marquée par un rôle plus discret. De son côté, la direction de l'OM maintient sa position. Le club conditionnerait le maintien du joueur à une baisse de son salaire, dans le cadre de sa politique de réduction de la masse salariale et de rééquilibrage de ses finances avant le début du nouvel exercice. Sous contrat avec Marseille, Amine Harit conserve donc sa priorité : poursuivre son parcours en Ligue 1. Toutefois, si aucun accord n'est trouvé sur le plan financier, la piste qatarie pourrait prendre de l'épaisseur dans les prochaines semaines, alors que le mercato estival entre dans une phase décisive. items.title: Luca Zidane : après un Mondial 2026 décevant, le gardien des Verts rejoint Leganés
items.description: L’aventure de Luca Zidan e avec Grenade FC s’est terminée officiellement ce vendredi 7 août. Après deux saisons passées dans le club andalou et une Coupe du monde décevante avec l’Algérie, le gardien international algérien de 28 ans a signé ce vendredi à Leganés, toujours en Espagne. L’annonce a été faite par ce club qui évolue en deuxième division du championnat espagnol. « Le CD Leganés a conclu un accord ce vendredi pour la signature du gardien de but Luca Zidane Fernández, âgé de 28 ans, pour un contrat d'un an assorti d'une option pour une deuxième année », a indiqué le club dans un communiqué. Leganés ne tarit pas d’éloges sur Luca Zidane Leganés n’a pas tari d’éloge sur le fils de Zinedine Zidane. « Gardien de but doté d'une technique, de réflexes et d'un jeu au pied exceptionnels, Luca rejoint Ontime Butarque pour poursuivre sa carrière », a écrit le club de la région de Madrid, qui rappelle que le portier des Fennecs a été formé au centre de formation du Real Madrid. Luca Zidane quitte ainsi le Grenade FC après deux saisons et à l’issue d’une Coupe du monde 2026 avec l’Algérie, où il n’a pas brillé, disputant trois matchs sur quatre et encaissant six buts : trois face à l’Argentine, un contre la Jordanie et deux face à la Suisse en 16 e de finale. Il a été très critiqué par les supporters et certains anciens joueurs pour ses prestations irrégulières. Face à l’Argentine au premier tour du Mondial 2026, il lui a été reproché d’avoir encaissé un but facile à repousser. items.title: GAUA resumes nationwide strike over pay disparities
items.description: The Ghana Association of University Administrators (GAUA) has announced the resumption of its suspended nationwide strike. The Association has directed members across Ghana’s public universities to stay away from work from Monday, August 10, until further notice over what it describes as widening pay disparities between teaching and non-teaching senior members. The decision was taken at the Association’s National Congress held in Sunyani on Friday, where delegates said recent adjustments to market premiums had created significant inequities despite teaching and non-teaching staff operating under the same analogous senior member structure. GAUA said it supports improvements in the conditions of service for teaching senior members but maintained that such gains should not come at the expense of non-teaching senior members. According to the Association, all senior members received a harmonised market premium of 114% when the Single Spine Salary Structure was introduced in 2012. Although an agreement signed with the government in April 2026 granted non-teaching senior members a 40% increase in consolidated market premium and non-basic allowances, GAUA said a substantial gap remains. The Association said teaching senior members now receive an average market premium of about GH¢10,000, compared with approximately GH¢4,718 for non-teaching senior members, a difference of about GH¢5,282. It argued that the disparity undermines fairness, internal equity and the objectives of the Single Spine Pay Policy. GAUA also expressed concern that the lowest-ranked teaching senior member, an assistant lecturer, now receives a higher market premium than the highest-ranked non-teaching senior member, such as a registrar or finance officer. The Association said it formally petitioned the National Labour Commission (NLC) and other state institutions on July 16, seeking intervention over the issue, but had not received a response. GAUA stressed that its action is not directed against teaching senior members but seeks equitable treatment for all senior members based on transparent and consistent principles. It called on the government and other stakeholders to address the disparities and uphold fairness in the remuneration of university staff. In announcing the industrial action, the Association directed all members to stay away from work until the issues in dispute are satisfactorily resolved.

items.title: Infrastructure vandalism: Scavengers threaten Lagos bridge, 27 arrested
items.description: By Olasunkanmi Akoni LAGOS — The Lagos State Government has uncovered alleged vandalism of critical infrastructure beneath the newly constructed bridge linking Festac Town with the Alakija area of Amuwo-Odofin Local Government Area of the state. The discovery was made during a special enforcement operation conducted by state government agencies in line with the directive of Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu to rid the Lagos-Badagry Transnational Highway of infractions, environmental pollution, illegal motor parks, roadside trading and unauthorised activities on highway setbacks and pedestrian walkways. The State Commissioner for the Environment and Water Resources, Tokunbo Wahab, disclosed the development on Friday through his official X handle. According to Wahab, preliminary investigations indicated that suspected vandals, including scavengers, had allegedly removed iron rods, steel reinforcements, cables and other materials from beneath the bridge. He said the alleged removal of the materials could compromise the structural integrity of the infrastructure and pose a safety concern to members of the public. “This criminal act poses a serious threat to public safety and undermines the government’s investment in critical infrastructure,” Wahab stated. Following the discovery, a joint midnight enforcement operation involving officers of the Rapid Response Squad (RRS) and the Kick Against Indiscipline (KAI) task force was launched at the location. The operation resulted in the arrest of 27 suspects, who Wahab said would be prosecuted in accordance with the extant laws of Lagos State. “The Lagos State Government remains committed to protecting public infrastructure and will continue to take decisive action against individuals or groups engaged in acts of vandalism, environmental infractions and other criminal activities that threaten the safety and wellbeing of residents,” he said. Residents condemn alleged vandalism Some residents who reacted to the development condemned the alleged vandalism and called for stricter enforcement and appropriate punishment for offenders. A resident identified as @Primax2U said government should also address some of the socio-economic factors that could encourage people to engage in scavenging and other activities to make a living. “As much as it’s bad destroying government property and risking lives, government needs to also assist in subsidising basic amenities or, better still, create job opportunities that would definitely remove more idle minds to more productive things than destruction to make a living,” the resident said. Another resident, identified as @tycityevents, expressed concern over the alleged removal of structural materials from beneath the bridge. “We have some terrible people in Lagos. How can anyone dig deep beneath a bridge just to remove the steel reinforcement rods? If urgent action isn’t taken, this bridge could be at serious risk,” the resident stated. Third Mainland Bridge The latest incident recalls similar cases of alleged vandalism reported on the Third Mainland Bridge, where suspects were arrested in connection with the removal of newly installed infrastructure. The Third Mainland Bridge has previously been targeted by vandals, with reports of the theft and destruction of safety installations, including solar-powered reflective road studs and bridge railings. Authorities subsequently intensified surveillance and patrols around the bridge, with CCTV systems also deployed to assist in identifying and tracking suspected offenders. The removal of road studs and reflective lighting installations can reduce visibility for motorists, particularly at night, potentially increasing road safety risks. The incidents have prompted condemnation from government officials and calls for stronger surveillance and protection of public infrastructure across Lagos. The post Infrastructure vandalism: Scavengers threaten Lagos bridge, 27 arrested appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Defence Minister-designate Adjei must prioritise GAF personnel welfare — KAIPTC lecturer
items.description: Security lecturer at the Kofi Annan International Peacekeeping Training Centre (KAIPTC), Dr Victor Doke, has urged Defence Minister-designate Kenneth Gilbert Adjei to make the welfare of personnel of the Ghana Armed Forces his foremost priority if approved by Parliament. Dr Doke made the remarks following President John Dramani Mahama’s decision to reassign Mr Adjei from the Ministry of Works, Housing and Water Resources to the Ministry of Defence. The appointment comes nearly a year after the death of Defence Minister Dr Edward Omane Boamah, who was among those killed in a military helicopter crash. President Mahama has submitted Mr Adjei’s nomination to Parliament through the Speaker for prior approval, in accordance with Article 78(1) of the 1992 Constitution. Speaking on the responsibilities awaiting the minister-designate, Dr Doke said addressing the welfare of military personnel should be at the centre of his agenda. READ ALSO: Mahama names Kenneth Gilbert Adjei as Defence Minister to replace late Omane Boamah “The welfare generally of the armed forces is a particular issue, is a top priority as at now, and housing, remuneration, promotions, the gender issues are top notch.” According to him, improving accommodation, remuneration, career progression and addressing gender-related concerns within the Armed Forces will be critical to strengthening morale and operational effectiveness. Dr Doke also said the minister-designate faces a significant task in succeeding his predecessor and will need to draw on the experience of both the military leadership and former officials to succeed. “It’s one of the issues which Honourable Gilbert would have to tackle as much as possible. He has a big, big, big position now, big shoes to fill. He needs to court all the cooperation and collaboration from the military hierarchy, past leaders of that specific agency and then get the ideas, the knowledge to be able to roll out the initiatives that he wants and then the objectives of the President for the Ghana Armed Forces.” He expressed confidence that the military’s leadership would support the incoming minister, regardless of who occupies the position, provided there is mutual respect and effective engagement. “The military hierarchy as I know is ready and willing to work with whoever has the nod. It’s how you relate to them, and give them that opportunity to perform their mandate per the Constitution.”

items.title: Última hora de la entrada de inmigrantes a Ceuta, en directo | Italia rechaza el ultimátum de España y mantendrá los controles a los viajeros hasta el 15 de agosto
items.description: El Gobierno establece de manera temporal los controles en las fronteras interiores de puertos y aeropuertos para los desplazamientos procedentes de Italia, ante la persistente presión migratoria irregular que sufre el país transalpino. Estos controles fronterizos estarán operativos a partir de la medianoche de este sábado, 8 de agosto. Italia ha rechazado este viernes el ultimátum del Gobierno español sobre los controles en su frontera para los viajeros procedentes de España tras la crisis de Ceuta. El Ejecutivo español había advertido previamente al de Georgia Meloni de que tomará “medidas proporcionales” si no retira la medida antes de este domingo. El ministro de Exteriores, José Manuel Albares, ha asegurado que “no hay ningún motivo” para que Italia mantenga los controles, ya que “la mayor parte de las personas que entraron irregularmente a Ceuta han sido ya devueltas”. Roma ha contestado en un comunicado que “no acepta ultimátums” y que no levantará los controles al menos hasta el 15 de agosto. Por otro lado, la ministra de Juventud e Infancia, Sira Rego, ha viajado a Ceuta para seguir trabajando en la acogida de los niños y adolescentes migrantes no acompañados que permanecen en la ciudad tras la entrada masiva del jueves de la semana pasada. Rego ha cifrado en 1.342 los menores registrados hasta el momento y ha asegurado que “van a ser atendidos todos”. “Ha habido una situación de desborde que ya se está controlando”, ha añadido. items.title: Tension à la BCRG : le syndicat menace de paralyser l’institution et accuse…
items.description: Le climat social se tend à la Banque centrale de la République de Guinée (BCRG). La délégation syndicale de l’institution, affiliée à l’Union syndicale des travailleurs de Guinée (USTG) et à la Fédération syndicale autonome des banques et assurances de Guinée (FESABAG), a annoncé ce vendredi 7 août 2026 le dépôt d’un préavis de grève, tout en dénonçant l’attitude des autorités actuelles de la BCRG. Lors d’un point de presse tenu à Conakry, les représentants des travailleurs ont confirmé avoir transmis, le jeudi 6 août, un préavis de grève à la direction générale de la BCRG. Le mouvement annoncé couvre la période du lundi 10 au jeudi 20 août 2026. À défaut d’un accord durant cette période, le syndicat menace de déclencher une grève générale illimitée jusqu’à la signature du protocole d’accord 2026. Selon le secrétaire général adjoint de la délégation syndicale, Aboubacar Sidiki Camara, ‘ ’cette décision fait suite au refus présumé du gouverneur de signer un protocole d’accord issu des négociations engagées autour de neuf points de revendication .’’ « Nous avons mené plusieurs démarches qui n’ont pas abouti. Les autorités refusent d’exécuter le protocole d’accord de 2026. Nous avions formulé des préalables prioritaires, notamment la prise en charge des évacuations sanitaires des employés. Malgré la validation de trois dossiers de malades, aucune suite n’a été donnée. Certains collègues sont décédés, d’autres sont devenus invalides. Nos camarades en détachement ont également été abandonnés », a déclaré le responsable syndical. Les travailleurs dénoncent également ce qu’ils qualifient de « blocages » dans le processus de négociation. « Un accord de principe avait pourtant été trouvé et un projet de protocole rédigé. Mais la signature a été retardée par plusieurs manœuvres. Des informations sur les revenus des employés auraient ensuite été collectées et diffusées sur les réseaux sociaux, ce qui met en danger l’image et la crédibilité de l’institution », a ajouté Aboubacar Sidiki Camara. S’appuyant sur les dispositions des articles 431.3 et suivants du Code du travail guinéen, la délégation syndicale indique avoir transmis une copie de sa notification à la FESABAG ainsi qu’à l’Inspection générale du travail (IGT). Elle appelle toutefois la direction de la BCRG à privilégier le dialogue afin d’éviter une escalade du conflit. « Nous invitons le cabinet à prendre les dispositions nécessaires pour trouver une issue favorable et constructive à cette situation et éviter un durcissement du mouvement syndical », a lancé le syndicat. Si aucun compromis n’est trouvé avant le 20 août, une paralysie de la Banque centrale pourrait avoir des conséquences importantes sur le fonctionnement du secteur bancaire et financier guinéen.

items.title: NELFUND disburses N303bn in student loans, urges North Central students to key in
items.description: By Edwin Philip, Lafia The Managing Director of the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), Dr Akintunde Sawyerr, has said that 850,000 individual Nigerians have benefited from President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s student loan scheme, with more than one million loan applications received and N303 billion disbursed within two years. The NELFUND managing director disclosed this on Friday at the Federal University of Lafia, Nasarawa State, during the Renewed Hope Students Leaders Engagement and Digital Acceleration Programme for the North Central Zone. Addressing participants, Sawyerr explained that President Bola Ahmed Tinubu had, for the first time in the history of the country, taken the financial burden of education off the shoulders of parents and students by ensuring that nobody misses the opportunity to acquire education because of lack of funds or sponsors. He said, “The President has recognised this and he said we cannot let young people just be roaming around the street for any reason, not because they don’t want to learn, but because they don’t have money or they don’t come from rich homes. The President said that is not acceptable.” He added: “He has deployed this programme known as NELFUND to ensure that if you want to get an education and harness your potential to be a great citizen, you must not be prevented from getting that opportunity simply because you come from a poor home.” The NELFUND boss charged students from the North Central region to key into the programme, stressing that applicants do not need to know anybody to access the loan, as all the information required to apply is available online. “The President has made money available. Just make sure you are qualified for it. The system he has allowed us to put in place is digital-based. If you want to get this loan, you don’t need to know anybody. It doesn’t matter who I am; you don’t need to know me, you don’t need to have my number, you don’t need to connect to me. “You go online and put in specific pieces of information that confirm that you qualify. “Your name, your BVN, your matriculation number, your JAMB registration number and date of birth. Make sure you are in a school that is approved, a government tertiary institution,” he said. He, however, appreciated the Senior Special Assistant to the President on Student Engagement, Comrade Asefon Sunday, for working tirelessly to drive the process and serve as a bridge between students and the government by ensuring that the mandate of NELFUND is achieved. On his part, the Minister of Education, Dr Maruf Tunji Alausa, represented by the Director of University Education, Federal Ministry of Education, Dr Kareem Olawale Lateef, said the student loan scheme reflected the administration’s commitment to investing in Nigerian students and preparing them for leadership, innovation, entrepreneurship and the digital economy. “The Renewed Hope Agenda recognises that the future of our nation depends on the quality, capacity and resilience of its young people. As a student, you are not only a leader of tomorrow, but an active partner in nation-building,” he said. In his address, the Senior Special Assistant to the President on Student Engagement, Comrade Asefon Sunday, charged student leaders to promote excellence, uphold integrity, encourage dialogue, and foster peace and coexistence within their institutions and communities. He pledged his continued commitment to engaging Nigerian students, listening to their aspirations and creating platforms that empower them academically, economically and socially. “President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has achieved a lot; he has done a lot for Nigerian students. As young people of this country who are leaders of today, we no longer call ourselves leaders of tomorrow. Enough is enough. Today, our universities and tertiary institutions are now celebrating three years of uninterrupted academic calendars because of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu,” he said. Speaking earlier, the Vice Chancellor of the Federal University of Lafia, Prof. Muhammed Isa Kida, said the event affirmed the government’s commitment to student development and engagement. He commended the students for their discipline and dedication, charging them not to indulge in practices and lifestyles that could undermine the efforts of the government to make them responsible citizens and future leaders. Participants were drawn from tertiary institutions across the North Central Zone of Nigeria. The post NELFUND disburses N303bn in student loans, urges North Central students to key in appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: GPHA announces urgent measures to ease congestion at Tema Port
items.description: The Ghana Ports and Harbours Authority (GPHA) has announced a series of urgent operational measures to address growing landside congestion at the Port of Tema, assuring stakeholders that efforts are underway to restore normal cargo flow and maintain efficient port operations. According to the Authority, the congestion has been driven largely by a significant increase in import volumes, a corresponding rise in exports of empty containers, and increasing road traffic challenges around the port enclave. GPHA noted that similar congestion related challenges are being experienced at several ports across the West African sub region, resulting in delays in container evacuations and the movement of both laden and empty containers. In response, the Authority said it has activated enhanced operational interventions and placed all relevant stakeholders on heightened operational alert. The measures are being implemented in close collaboration with shipping lines and terminal operators to improve cargo movement and maximise available terminal capacity. Among the key interventions are efforts to accelerate the evacuation of empty containers through increased vessel calls, strengthen container transfer operations, deploy additional trucks, improve the handling and storage of empty containers, and optimise yard and traffic management systems within the port. The Authority emphasised that these measures are designed to reduce congestion, improve efficiency, and ensure the uninterrupted flow of international trade through Ghana’s largest seaport. GPHA has also appealed to importers, clearing agents, and cargo owners to expedite the clearance and evacuation of their consignments from the port. The Authority stressed that the prompt removal of cargo is critical to creating additional space within terminals, enhancing operational efficiency, and facilitating the smooth movement of goods. “Prompt cargo evacuation remains essential to easing pressure on terminal space and supporting the continuous flow of trade through the port,” the Authority said. GPHA further assured stakeholders that it is closely monitoring developments and will continue to implement the necessary interventions to address the situation and restore normal operating conditions as quickly as possible. The Authority expressed appreciation to the trading community and the general public for their patience, cooperation, and understanding during the period of congestion. GPHA reiterated its commitment to maintaining a safe, efficient, and competitive port system capable of supporting Ghana’s international trade ambitions and broader economic growth objectives.

items.title: Tinubu tasks WEC Nigeria on global energy leadership
items.description: By Obas Esiedesa, Abuja President Bola Tinubu has tasked the newly inaugurated World Energy Council (WEC) Nigeria leadership with positioning the country as a leading voice in global energy affairs and ensuring that Africa’s perspectives shape international energy decisions. Tinubu gave the charge while welcoming Nigeria’s formal admission as the newest National Member Committee of the WEC, describing the development as a proud moment for the country and a strong vote of confidence in its energy reforms and leadership role in Africa. The President, in a statement issued on Friday by his Special Adviser on Information and Strategy, Bayo Onanuga, said Nigeria’s entry into the century-old global energy network of more than 100 countries would enable the country to play a more active role in shaping global discussions on energy security, equity and sustainability. “Nigeria has joined the World Energy Council to lead, not just participate – to ensure Africa’s voice shapes global energy decisions,” Tinubu said. Nigeria’s return to the WEC comes with a newly constituted National Member Committee and Governing Board, with the Nigerian chapter expected to strengthen the country’s engagement in global energy policymaking and help attract investment for energy transition and industrial development. The WEC Nigeria platform is designed as an independent, impartial and technology-neutral forum bringing together government, industry, financial institutions, academia and civil society to address the country’s energy priorities. Its work will focus on Nigeria’s Energy Trilemma of energy security, energy access and environmental sustainability, while supporting efforts to expand electricity access, strengthen energy security, accelerate gas development and mobilise investment for sustainable economic growth. The Council said Nigeria’s membership would also connect local businesses and institutions to international knowledge, technologies, partnerships and investment opportunities through its network of more than 3,000 member organisations across over 100 countries. Tinubu congratulated the inaugural leadership of WEC Nigeria, led by Abdulrazaq Isa as Chairman and Bala Wunti as Chief Executive Officer, as well as members of the inaugural Board drawn from across the energy value chain, regulatory institutions, industry associations, finance, academia and the Future Energy Leaders community. The President described Isa as a distinguished patriot and industrialist whose investments in indigenous refining and industrial energy had opened a new frontier for Nigerian enterprise. He described Wunti as an energy strategist and reform advocate whose more than three decades of service had been marked by reforms aimed at strengthening national revenues and investor confidence in the energy sector. Tinubu said the combination of industry leaders, regulators, finance experts and youth leaders on the Board would provide the balance, neutrality and credibility required for WEC Nigeria to succeed. He affirmed the full support of the Federal Government for WEC Nigeria as a neutral, technology-agnostic platform for policy dialogue, investment mobilisation and innovation. The President also reiterated Nigeria’s commitment to working with WEC London and its global community to deliver secure, affordable and sustainable energy for all. He wished the Chairman, CEO and members of the inaugural Board success in what he described as a historic national assignment. The post Tinubu tasks WEC Nigeria on global energy leadership appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Rethinking assessment, achievement and ranking in Ghanaian education
items.description: WHEN THE RULER BECOMES THE RACE Rethinking Assessment, Achievement and Ranking in Ghanaian Education A Nunyãdume Reflection on What Our Examinations Should Actually Measure The Elders of Nunyãdume tell of a teacher who gathered ten children beneath the village tree and taught them to climb. At the end of the year, nine could climb the tree. The villagers celebrated. But the examiner shook his head. “ If nine have reached the top, ” he asked, “ how shall I know which child is first? “ So he measured how quickly each child climbed. One reached the top first. Another came second. Someone necessarily came ninth. And the tenth did not reach the top at all. The examiner proudly announced that he had successfully ranked the children. An Elder sitting nearby asked: “ But was our purpose to discover who could climb, or merely who climbed faster than another? “ The village became quiet. That question, I believe, deserves to be asked about Ghanaian education. What is the purpose of education? Education must certainly identify excellence. Universities and competitive programmes must select among applicants. Scholarships must sometimes distinguish among candidates. Schools with fewer places than applicants require mechanisms for selection. Ranking therefore has a legitimate place in education. But ranking is not education . And ranking is not the same thing as measuring learning. There is a fundamental distinction between the two questions: Has this child achieved the educational standard we established? and How did this child perform compared with other children? The first measures achievement . The second establishes relative position . Both questions can be legitimate. But they are not the same question. Our difficulty begins when we ask one examination grade to answer both. The BECE Paradox WAEC states explicitly that BECE candidates are graded using the stanine ( STA ndard NINE ), a method of scaling test scores on a nine-point standard scale with a mean of 5 and a standard deviation of 2. The earliest known use of stanine was by the U.S. Army Air Forces in 1942. More importantly, WAEC explains why: the system was considered appropriate for the dual purposes of certification and selection . WAEC further explains that stanine grading ranks and compares candidates’ performances relative to one another. Indeed, WAEC has explained that BECE does not operate with fixed grade boundaries in the ordinary sense; boundaries may vary according to candidate performance. There is nothing psychometrically illegitimate about norm-referenced assessment. The question is whether we are asking it to perform a task for which a different form of assessment may be more appropriate. Ghana’s curriculum philosophy increasingly emphasises competencies and performance standards . Our National Pre-Tertiary Education Curriculum Framework describes assessment as determining how far a learner has attained necessary knowledge, skills, attitudes and behaviours, and emphasises that, assessment should provide meaningful feedback about progress toward defined performance indicators. This presents us with an intellectually important question: If our curriculum is increasingly standards- and competency-oriented, should our principal assessment philosophy not also tell us whether those standards and competencies have actually been achieved? The Difference Between Achievement and Ranking Imagine that Ghana decides that every child completing JHS should be able to solve a particular level of mathematical problem. We invest in teachers. We improve textbooks. We introduce technology. We support struggling pupils. And eventually 90 per cent of our children master that competency. That should constitute a national educational triumph. A criterion-referenced assessment can tell us: Nine out of every ten Ghanaian children have attained the required mathematical competency. A norm-referenced system asks a different question: Which children performed better than the others? Even in an outstanding cohort, somebody remains at the bottom. Conversely, if an entire cohort performs badly, relative ranking can still identify its highest performers. That information is useful for selection . It is considerably less useful for determining whether Ghana’s educational system is actually succeeding. The distinction is fundamental: A nation should measure its children principally against what it promised to teach them, not merely against one another. The Mental-Health Question Why should the Chief Executive of the Mental Health Authority enter a discussion about educational assessment? Because examinations do not merely produce grades. They produce experiences. They influence identity. They influence family expectations. They influence anxiety. They influence self-worth. And, for some young people, they appear to determine their entire future. A child can easily move psychologically from: “I performed poorly in an examination” to: “I am a failure.” Those statements are profoundly different. One describes an outcome. The other defines a human being. An educational system must be demanding. Standards matter. Excellence matters. Competition will sometimes be unavoidable. But unnecessary competition should never masquerade as educational measurement. Educational psychologists, psychiatrists, teachers and policymakers should therefore ask not whether examinations cause some anxiety, that is inevitable, but whether the architecture of assessment unnecessarily transforms learning into perpetual social comparison . What, then, should Ghana do? I propose neither the abolition of BECE nor the abandonment of ranking. I propose something more conceptually coherent: Separate Certification from Selection. Certification should answer: “What has the learner mastered?” At both BECE and WASSCE levels, Ghana should progressively establish clearly defined, criterion-referenced competency standards. A grade should communicate meaningful information such as: Advanced proficiency. Proficient. Developing proficiency. Basic attainment. Below expected standard. The boundaries should be anchored, as far as psychometrically feasible, to what candidates demonstrably know and can do. The nation could then meaningfully compare educational outcomes across years. If Mathematics proficiency rises from 45% to 75%, Ghana should be able to celebrate that achievement without requiring some predetermined proportion of children to occupy lower categories. Selection should answer: “Where does the learner rank when places are scarce?” Where 20,000 qualified children compete for 5,000 places, ranking becomes necessary. Use an appropriate standardised score, percentile, placement index or other psychometrically defensible mechanism for that particular purpose . But call it what it is: selection. Do not confuse it with mastery. Thus a learner could receive: Mathematics: Proficient and, where necessary for competitive placement: National/placement percentile: 78th One tells the family what the child knows. The other tells the system where that child stands in a competition for scarce places. BECE and WASSCE should share one assessment philosophy; not necessarily identical grades This is where I would modify the proposition that started this discussion. I would not insist that BECE and WASSCE must necessarily use identical grading symbols. Their purposes and developmental stages differ. I would insist on something more important: From basic education through senior high school, Ghana should have one intelligible philosophy: achievement is measured against defined educational standards; ranking is separately reported when selection requires it. That creates continuity without forcing artificial uniformity. The Two Princesses of Nunyãdume The Stammering Linguist of Nunyãdume tells of two young princesses whose educational journey did not follow the familiar road. When other children travelled the conventional path towards the BECE, these two were educated for a period within the compound of the Chief Linguist. There were no school bells to announce the beginning of lessons. There were no positions in class to tell them whether they were first, fifth or fiftieth. But there were books. There was discipline. There was curiosity. There were expectations. There were examinations of another kind, the daily expectation that what had been taught must be understood, questioned and applied. And eventually, when the princesses left the compound and entered the larger educational world, something interesting happened. The absence of a BECE certificate had not meant the absence of learning. They progressed. They competed. And eventually, both gained admission to study medicine in Ghana. If Odomankoma , the Creator, grants them life and good health, they may in the coming years emerge as young doctors serving their country. The Elders of Nunyãdume did not tell this story to argue that Ghanaian children should be homeschooled. Neither did they suggest that two princesses constitute scientific evidence. Two children cannot establish national educational policy. Nor should an educational opportunity available to one family automatically be assumed feasible, appropriate or equitable for millions of Ghanaian families. The Elders told the story because it forced Nunyãdume to confront a more fundamental question: Is passing through every conventional examination necessarily synonymous with learning? The experience of the two princesses suggests that the answer cannot simply be yes . For an examination is an instrument for measuring education . It is not education itself. A weighing scale can tell the farmer something about his harvest. But the scale did not grow the maize. Likewise, an examination can tell us something important about what a child has learned. But sitting an examination did not, by itself, produce the learning. And ranking children tells us something else again. It tells us how one child performed relative to another . It does not necessarily tell us whether either child has attained the standard Ghana expected them to achieve. That distinction is fundamental. The Elders therefore asked: “If ten children reach the top of the tree, does the fact that one arrived tenth mean that child cannot climb?” Surely NOT . And if none of the ten reaches the top, does declaring one of them first mean that the village has successfully taught its children to climb? Surely NOT . Therein lies the distinction between achievement and ranking . Our educational system must first determine whether the learner has acquired the knowledge, competencies and intellectual tools we promised to teach. Where opportunities are scarce and selection becomes necessary, we may then ask who performed better than whom. But we should never confuse the second question with the first. For the ultimate purpose of education cannot simply be to determine which child stands above another . It must be to enable every child to stand . And perhaps that is the lesson the two princesses unknowingly taught Nunyãdume: There may be many roads to learning, but every road must eventually be judged by what the traveller knows, understands and can do, not merely by whether the traveller passed the same milestone as everyone else. The role of educational psychologists I believe Ghana’s educational psychologists should occupy the intellectual centre of this conversation. This should not become a political contest between those “for” and “against” WAEC. WAEC performs an indispensable national and regional function. Nor should politicians alone determine the answer. This is fundamentally a question of psychometrics, developmental psychology, pedagogy, curriculum design, equity, and public policy. Educational psychologists should help Ghana determine: What exactly does each examination purport to measure? Are grades valid measures of those constructs? What competencies constitute satisfactory attainment? How should standards be set? How stable should those standards remain across cohorts? When is norm-referencing appropriate? When is criterion-referencing preferable? What is the psychological effect of high-stakes ranking? How do socioeconomic inequalities influence apparent merit? How should school-based assessment complement external examinations? And how can assessment produce information that improves teaching rather than merely sorting children? NaCCA’s own mandate includes developing national curriculum and assessment standards and reviewing national assessments, making such a multidisciplinary reconsideration institutionally compatible with Ghana’s existing educational architecture. From examination system to learning system The Elders of Nunyãdume say: “When the farmer weighs his harvest, the scale does not make the maize grow.” Examinations are scales. They are important. They tell us something about the harvest. But weighing children more frequently does not educate them. Ranking them more precisely does not necessarily make them more competent. Our real national questions are harder: Can they read with understanding? Can they reason mathematically? Can they interrogate evidence? Can they communicate? Can they collaborate? Can they create? Can they solve unfamiliar problems? Can they disagree without becoming enemies? Can they use knowledge ethically? Can they continue learning after the examiner has left the room? If the answer is yes, education has succeeded, even if another child happens to be better. If the answer is no, a Grade 1 cannot rescue the system. A National Assessment Compact I would therefore propose that Ghana convene a technically led National Assessment Compact , bringing together NaCCA, WAEC, GES, the Ministry of Education, universities, Colleges of Education, educational psychologists, psychometricians, teachers, parents, students, mental-health professionals, and employers. Its mandate should not begin with: “Should we abolish stanines?” That prematurely prescribes the answer. It should begin with: “What information should Ghana’s national examinations provide about every child, and for what purpose?” Only after answering that question should we choose the measurement instruments. That is how science should inform policy. The Child Is More Than the Rank The Elders of Nunyãdume return finally to those ten children beneath the baobab tree. The examiner had arranged them from first to tenth. Then the Elder asked the child who came ninth: “Can you climb?” The child answered: “Yes.” “Then why,” asked the Elder, “have we spent the whole afternoon discussing the eight children who climbed before you?” There lies the philosophical heart of the matter. Ranking tells us who came before whom. Assessment should first tell us who can climb. And education must ultimately teach every child to climb. Ghana should therefore pursue an assessment system rigorous enough to recognise excellence, sensitive enough to identify difficulty, fair enough to accommodate different pathways, and intelligent enough to distinguish achievement from competition . Let us measure our children against high standards. Let us identify exceptional achievement. Where scarce opportunities require ranking, let us rank transparently and scientifically. But let us never confuse a child’s position in a distribution with the measure of that child’s potential. For the Elders of Nunyãdume say: “The fact that one bird flies higher does not mean the others have forgotten how to fly.” Our educational system should tell every Ghanaian child: how well they have learned, what they can do, where they need help, and how they can improve. Only after that, where necessity demands it, should we ask who came first. That is the difference between an educational system designed principally to sort children and one designed to develop them. And Ghana must choose development.

items.title: ‘Do I look like someone who can be bullied?’ – Agalga dismisses doubts over possible Majority Leader role
items.description: Builsa North legislator, James Agalga, has brushed aside suggestions that he could be intimidated in a possible role as Majority Leader. He insisted that his years of parliamentary experience have adequately prepared him to lead the business of the House. The MP said his experience as a Ranking Member, Committee Chairman and long-serving legislator has equipped him with the leadership skills required to serve as Majority Leader. His remarks come in response to comments by former Defence Minister and Minority Leader Dominic Nitiwul, who questioned his leadership credentials. Mr Nitiwul argued that although Mr Agalga is among the longest-serving Members of Parliament, he had not previously occupied one of the House’s top leadership positions. Responding to the criticism, Mr Agalga said he was confident his performance would ultimately determine how Ghanaians assess his leadership. “I think that the end shall justify the means. Do I look like somebody who can be bullied?” he asked on Accra-based Citi FM on August 7. “We leave the rest for the people to judge when we settle down to work.” He rejected claims that he lacks leadership experience in Parliament, pointing to the various positions he has held over the years. “I want to assure you that I am not new to leadership in Parliament. I have been ranking member for eight solid years. I am currently the chairman of the Defence and Interior Committee. And so, to that extent, it cannot be said that I am new to leadership,” he said. Mr Agalga further argued that his long tenure in Parliament has earned him the respect of his colleagues, making suggestions that he could be bullied unfounded. “I am a full-term Member of Parliament. And so, I do not think that any colleague of mine in the House can bully me,” he said. He maintained that the true measure of his leadership would only become evident when Parliament resumes sitting and his stewardship is put to the test. “But like I said, the end shall justify the means,” he added.

items.title: The Genre That’s a Shortcut to Wisdom
items.description: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books. Sign up for it here. “How are you on theory ?” my editor asked me earlier this week. I knew what he was talking about—not my pet hypotheses about, say, the existence of cryptids, but rather a group of 20th-century French philosophers. Yet I didn’t know much else beyond that. I was familiar with Michel Foucault, partly from college coursework but largely from a popular meme that features his most famous concept, the panopticon . I know about Roland Barthes and the death of the author. I know that Derrida, Lacan, and Deleuze are names that I should know. “Not good,” I told him. First, here are four new stories from The Atlantic’s Books section: Icarus in the faculty lounge Someone is mysteriously snapping up used books around the world. What if Freud was right? “Out Here,” a collection of poems by the Black Seed Writers Group I could read their works for myself, of course. I could pick up Foucault’s Discipline and Punish at any one of the college bookstores that serve four major universities in my city. But frankly—and I don’t think I’m alone in this—I’d rather not. My preference as a busy adult is to begin my approach to foundational, complicated ideas with the help of a particular kind of book: the intellectual biography. The structuralists would hate this. Lynn Steger Strong makes exactly that point in an Atlantic essay published this week about a new group biography of these thinkers. I may be oversimplifying their ideas (as Strong writes, any “smooth summary inevitably sacrifices complexity”), but in general, they disregarded biography as a source of useful information about art; Barthes, especially, rejected literary criticism that drew on an author’s life to unlock the meaning of their work. “There was only the text, over which the writer had little control,” Strong explains. “Even the self was ultimately an unstable text.” This makes a biography of the cohort feel almost sacreligious. Emily Eakin’s new book, The Frenchmen , focuses on these men’s personal lives to illuminate their earthshaking writings. After finishing it, Strong wonders: “How could biography not be important?” I agree. Important ideas don’t just come to Earth fully formed and then flow through their speakers; they’re influenced by the wider context in which they develop. Earlier this year, when I was curious about the life and work of Karl Marx, the first book I reached for wasn’t Capital . Instead, I read Francis Wheen’s 2000 biography of the man —yes, I learned, he did ask Frederich Engels for money immediately after Engels told him that his beloved partner, Mary, had died. And yes, he really did spend ages in the British Museum’s reading room trying to squeeze as much information as possible into Capital (which is not to say that he didn’t miss anything). The biography also reminded me that Marx did not invent socialism; he was building on an intellectual tradition that predated him by decades. I encourage readers to try this out for themselves. Back in 2022, Talya Zax recommended nine group biographies that explain not only the lives of their subjects but also how those individuals influenced other people and movements. Personally, I’m on to a new topic: I’m about five chapters into Kai Bird and Susan Goldmark’s forthcoming biography of Roy Cohn, American Scoundrel , and the world of 20th-century New York City—an environment that incubated hundreds of famous and influential leaders, including our current president—is unfolding before me. Illustration by The Atlantic * How Theory Took Over the World By Lynn Steger Strong The French writers of the postwar era argued that the author’s life is irrelevant. Emily Eakin’s lively new book proves them wrong. Read the full article. What to Read The Haçienda: How Not to Run a Club , by Peter Hook The Haçienda in Manchester was a catalyst of the U.K. acid house scene in the late ’80s, and a prophecy foretold: “The haçienda must be built,” the Situationist poet Ivan Chtcheglov wrote in 1953. Heeding these cryptic words some three decades later, the audacious (and well-read) impresario Tony Wilson opened the Haçienda together with the circle of post-punk musicians and designers involved with his label, Factory Records. Their attempt to decipher Chtcheglov’s mystical phrase lasted 15 years. Hook, the bassist for New Order, served as a kind of player-coach at the Haçienda, helping manage its madcap affairs while his band became the club’s cash cow. In this memoir of misbegotten business administration, Hook returns to the storied nights out that changed British culture even as they threatened to bankrupt him—and worse. Beset by gangs and guns, the Haçienda faltered in the ’90s despite clever-sounding schemes such as replacing the club’s security with the gangsters themselves. This is a scrapbook of utopian folly, yes, but also an insider’s look at what was, for a time, the wildest workplace on Earth. — Andrew Holter From our list: Five books about going out that are worth staying in for Out Next Week 📚 Sunrise , by Téa Obreht 📚 Days of Miracle and Wonder: Paul Simon and the Trials and Triumphs of Graceland , by Ashley Kahn 📚 Under the Falls , by Richard Russo Your Weekend Read Will Oliver / Bloomberg / Getty Do Not Paint Granite! By Dorothy Robyn History and aesthetics aside, Trump’s plan violates a key rule of building maintenance : Do not paint granite. Granite is a superior building facade that has been used for other distinctive structures in Washington, D.C., such as the Library of Congress and the Old Post Office. Left unpainted, granite requires little maintenance. Once granite is painted, however (and examples are rare), it requires extensive maintenance in perpetuity. Greg Werkheiser, a co-founder of Cultural Heritage Partners , a law firm representing the DC Preservation League (which is suing over the project), has warned that the EEOB could become the Golden Gate Bridge of federal buildings : As soon as painting is finished on one end, it will be time to begin again on the other. Read the full article. When you buy a book using a link in this newsletter, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic .
